since they are both transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*)—the former being provisional and the latter being real—if one considers the various *saṃbhogakāya* Buddhas and *nirmāṇakāya* Buddhas, they do not transform those of the two vehicles, and it is not necessarily the case that these Buddhas appear in the world only during times of turbidity, whether their initial manifestation is provisional or their final nature is real.

If the transformation of the two vehicles involves an initial provisional [teaching] followed by a final reality, it must appear during a period of turbidity, because beings born in such evil times are difficult to transform and enter the Path only gradually.

This term "turbidity" refers to the period within the *apacayakalpa* (the eon of decrease) when these five [corruptions] gradually arise; thus, Maitreya Buddha will appear only when the human lifespan has gradually decreased from eighty thousand years toward the five turbidities. Therefore, it is not necessary for the "kalpa-turbidity" (*kalpakaṣāya*) to be defined solely as the time when minor calamities arise when the human lifespan is twenty or thirty years. Thus, various treatises state: "Buddhas appear in the world during the decrease of the kalpa; during the increase, a Wheel-Turning King appears."
Question:

If Buddhas appear in the world only during the period of kalpa-decrease (saṃvarta-kalpa), while Wheel-turning Kings (cakravartin) appear during the period of kalpa-increase (vivarta-kalpa), why do King Śaṅkha and Maitreya exist in the same era?

Furthermore, it is said that if the Buddha had not left the household life, he would have become a Wheel-turning King; likewise, the eight sons of Candrasūryapradīpa all ruled over the four continents. How is this so?

Answer: He appears during the period of increase in the *Rāśikha* eon; because his lifespan is long, he encounters Maitreya. It is not that Maitreya Buddha does not appear during a period of decrease.
Furthermore, had the Buddha not left the household life, he would have occupied the position of a Golden Wheel-turning King (*cakravartin*), yet this was not fixed.
The principle regarding the eight sons of Dīpaṃkara is the same; since they were *vipākakāya* (retribution bodies), that fault does not apply.

It is said that a Golden Wheel-turning King necessarily appears during a period of increase (*vivarta-kalpa*), whereas the appearance of Silver, Copper, and Iron Wheel-turning Kings is not fixed. Thus, in the era of King Aśoka, one hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there was an Iron Wheel-turning King.
Regarding the sūtra passage from “In this way, Śāriputra” up to “differentiate and explain the three,” the commentary states:

The following explains the reasons for the appearance of a Buddha amidst the five corruptions (*pañca kaṣāyāḥ*). It cites and points back to the previously indicated subject of the five corruptions that are to be explained; therefore, it says “in this way.”

Regarding the phrase "during the period of the turbulence of the kalpa-impurity," this restates the preceding "kalpa-impurity" as the time when famine, pestilence, and weapons arise. Regarding "the defilements of sentient beings are heavy," this restates the "sentient-being impurity."

"Defilements" (*mala*) refers to the six defilements; because they pollute the body and mind and stain them with impurity, they are called "defilements. Because they are intensified and difficult to destroy, they are called "heavy. These are: (1) malice (*āghāta*), (2) resentment (*upanāha*), (3) vexation (*pradāsa*), (4) guile (*śāṭhya*), (5) deceit (*māyā*), and (6) arrogance (*mada*). Among these, that which takes pleasure in harming sentient beings is called "malice."
Preceded by anger (*krodha*), the failure to relinquish a grudge is called resentment (*upanāha*).

Having pursued past evils, when encountering adverse conditions in the present, the mind becomes perverse and stubborn; the frequent utterance of clamorous, violent, wicked, base, and coarse words that sting like a gadfly is called vexation (*pradāśa*).
These three have hatred as their essence.
To ensnare others, to conceal what one has lost, or to adopt a deceptive outward appearance to win over another's mind—this crookedness is called *śāṭhya* (hypocrisy).

To feign the possession of virtues for the sake of profit and reputation is called "deceit" (*śāṭhya*); that is to say, a deceitful person harbors ulterior motives and frequently manifests unreal matters as a form of wrong livelihood.
These two have greed and delusion as their essential nature.
*Mada* (intoxication/arrogance) refers to the deep arising of defiled attachment and haughty pride toward one's own prosperity; it has greed as its essential nature.
Because the six stains of sentient beings are heavy, and because they do not recognize śramaṇas nor cultivate wholesome dharmas, this is the *sattva-kaṣāya* (degeneration of sentient beings).
Avarice, greed, and envy constitute the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*).
To be attached to wealth and teachings already acquired and unable to give them away is called stinginess (*mātsarya*).
To long for various things not yet obtained, as well as the means to obtain them, is called greed (*lobha*).

Although stinginess (*mātsarya*) is itself a form of greed (*lobha*), it is established as a separate category because its defiled longing differs from that for what has already been acquired versus what has not yet been acquired.

As for "envy" (*īrṣyā*): its phonetic transcriptions are *qín xī*, *qín xuè*, or *cí lì* (the latter three being pronounced with the third tone); alternatively, it is written as *jiàn* or *jí*, meaning malice or harm.
To sacrifice oneself for fame and profit, to be unable to endure the glory of others, and to harbor envy, resentment, and sorrow—this is called *īrṣyā* (envy).

Although *īrṣyā* is synonymous with *mātsarya* (jealousy), it is termed *īrṣyā* when directed toward another's correct Dharma, and it is termed *mātsarya* when directed toward another's prosperity, happiness, fame, or profit.
The *Shuowen* and the *Yupian* state: "To harm the worthy is called *jí* (envy); to harm [the beauty of] others is called *dù* (jealousy).
Regarding "accomplishing all unwholesome roots," there are three unwholesome roots:
namely, greed (*lobha*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and delusion (*moha*).

The unwholesome roots (*akuśalamūla*) are established by virtue of possessing two characteristics: first, they are fundamental afflictions (*mūlakleśa*) capable of giving rise to others; this excludes the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), which cannot be so established.

Second, they are present throughout all six consciousnesses and possess faults that are profound and extensive; other factors such as pride (*māna*), views (*dṛṣṭi*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*) are not unwholesome roots because they exist only in the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Because they possess these two characteristics, only three are designated as unwholesome roots (*akuśalamūla*).
"Root" (*mūla*) carries the meaning of "origination," as they give rise to adverse conditions for evil; they are also identical to the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśakaṣāya*).

Only the three turbidities are mentioned and not the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭikaṣāya*) or the turbidity of lifespan (*āyuṣkaṣāya*), because the turbidity of the eon (*kalpakaṣāya*) subsumes the turbidity of lifespan, as lifespans are generally short due to famine, warfare, and disease.
The defilement of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*) subsumes the views and the unwholesome roots, because it subsumes the very root of all afflictions.

At that time, as humans and devas diminished and those in the evil realms increased, it was difficult for sentient beings to be taught and transformed by means of the Mahāyāna all at once. Therefore, through the skillful means of wisdom, the single Buddha-vehicle was differentiated and taught as three, so that they might gradually enter the Path. Thus, the sutra below states: "He only praised the Buddha-vehicle, yet sentient beings, submerged in suffering, were unable to believe and accept it"; therefore, he taught by means of skillful expedients.
Regarding the passage from "Śāriputra... up to not a pratyekabuddha," the commentary states:
From here below, the second doubt is explained.
The second doubt states: "If the Tathāgata does not teach for those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*), how is it known that they possess such pride?
This section contains three parts:

first, revealing the characteristics of those who are not true *śrāvaka* āryas; second, revealing the characteristics of those with overweening pride; and third, concluding by establishing the characteristics of the two types of true āryas.
This is the first passage.

Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who have truly entered the noble path toward tranquility will, for the most part, not remain ignorant of the Dharma if they encounter a Buddha. As for those of indeterminate lineage who are capable of turning their minds [toward the Mahāyāna], regardless of whether it takes long or short, they will certainly be able to hear and know the deeds of the Buddhas’ transformation of bodhisattvas; therefore, it is so named.

Claiming for themselves to be these two holy sages who have encountered the Buddha, they are entirely unaware of the matter of the transformation bodhisattvas; they are neither the holy disciples of the Buddha, nor are they truly the two holy sages.
The Sūtra states: “Furthermore, Śāriputra... [omitted] ...they are all people of overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
The commentary says:
This reveals the characteristics of those with overweening pride.

When an ordinary person attains the fourth dhyāna but has not yet abandoned the defilements of the three realms, they claim for themselves that they are truly among the two types of noble ones, that this is their final body as an arhat, and that they have attained ultimate nirvana; yet they do not seek perfect enlightenment and lack faith and inclination toward it—this is overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
Regarding the passage from "Why is this so? to "there is no such possibility," the commentary states:
This concludes the characteristics of the two types of noble ones.

However, those who are true noble ones and encounter me are for the most part those who incline toward tranquility and are not persons of non-dharma; although they may be unable to practice, they believe upon hearing [the teaching], for because they possess the lineage of the indeterminate, they rationally believe in and cultivate awakening, and are thus truly the two types of noble ones.
If they were to lack faith, it would be impossible, as that would contradict the principle.

Those who incline toward tranquility are unable to enter [this realization]; at first they do not believe, which is termed "diminishment through alarm. Doubt arises as they turn back from the path, but later they will certainly believe it, thereby becoming established in the Dharma of non-delusion. Therefore, this concluding statement says: "It is impossible that one would not believe in the One Vehicle."
The Sūtra states: "Except after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, when no Buddha is present.
The Commentary says:
From here below, the third doubt is explained: how can one be capable of preaching?

This refers to those who harbor doubts, saying that having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, they give rise to a mind of slander, asking: "How could the Tathāgata not be one capable of teaching the Dharma?

The meaning of this is that even those who have entered the two noble paths of tranquility (*śama*) and reality (*tattva*), yet remain ignorant of the Dharma, may hear the teaching and give rise to slander; furthermore, the fact that they do not hear or know [the teaching] but are merely transformed by Bodhisattvas is precisely because the World-Honored One was unable to transform them.
Why would the Buddha not become one incapable of preaching the Dharma?

Since he has indeed become such a person, the text reverses the phrasing to ask: how could the World-Honored One be capable of preaching the Dharma for sentient beings and yet be called "One Possessing All-Knowledge"?

Therefore, the Buddha replied: "Except for after my parinirvāṇa when no Buddha is present before them, those who truly enter into tranquility but encounter me will for the most part not be deluded regarding the Dharma; they will all certainly hear and know that [the disciples] were merely transformed bodhisattvas.
However, those who enter into tranquility without encountering me may be deluded regarding the Dharma, and thus would be unable to know that they were merely transformed bodhisattvas."
This passage consists of three parts:
first, the heading; second, the explanation; and third, the conclusion.
This is the first part.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "For what reason? up to "such a person is difficult to find," the commentary states:
This explains the preceding heading.

After my parinirvāṇa, because they will be led by no virtuous conditions or skillful means, many among those who have entered the tranquility of the various realms of existence will be deluded regarding the Dharma. For such individuals, it will be difficult to receive, uphold, and understand the meaning of these sūtras, as they do not comprehend their intent.
Therefore, after my parinirvāṇa, there will be true and second-tier noble ones who, having neither heard nor known [these teachings], shall transform only bodhisattvas.
The Sūtra says: "If one encounters another Buddha, one will immediately attain definitive understanding.
The Commentary states:
This concludes the preceding meaning.

These deluded followers of the Dharma, if they encounter another Buddha after my parinirvāṇa who teaches through skillful means and transformation, will then attain definitive understanding within this Dharma; thus, they too will be able to know that [the teaching] was merely for the sake of transforming bodhisattvas.
Those who do not encounter a Buddha, however, will remain ignorant. Therefore, it is not that I am currently incapable of speaking [of this], and so forth.
Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:

"If the ālayavijñāna has already been established, then even when one enters the meditative absorption of cessation within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), one must believe that the storehouse consciousness exists and is not interrupted."

Or again, this doubt may be a non-doubt that tends toward tranquility; since doubt and overweening pride are not transformed, how could the World-Honored One not be one who is incapable of teaching the Dharma?

Therefore, this commentary states: "I shall certainly transform them until their afflictions are eliminated after my parinirvāṇa," and so forth, up to the passage in the Sūtra from "Śāriputra" to "the single Buddha-vehicle.
The commentary says:
The following passage explains the fourth doubt: "Previously, the three vehicles were taught, whereas now they are taught as one; thus, the teaching now is different.
Since the teaching now is different, how is it that the World-Honored One does not commit the offense of false speech?"

Therefore, the Buddha replied: "I have already realized and understood it, whereas you know nothing at all; your stage of practice has not yet reached it. You should simply believe with single-mindedness what I have said, for when you first resolve your mind [for enlightenment], you are initially worthy of faith. Even an Arhat who turns his mind [toward Buddhahood] takes twenty thousand kalpas before reaching the initial stage of faith at the beginning of the three great asaṃkhyeya-kalpas. Thus, you should only believe and not give rise to doubt."

The Buddha’s words are without falsehood, and the principle is solely that of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Since those of indeterminate lineage ultimately achieve the fruit of gnosis, there is likewise only the One Vehicle and no second vehicle.

Thus, the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The four things spoken of by the Buddha are without falsehood: enlightenment, the prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*), the Hīnayāna, and the Mahāyāna. As this refers here to the Mahāyāna and the prophecy, it establishes his speech as non-false.

At the very beginning of this chapter, there was already a section on "Resolving Doubts" (*nirṇaya*) following the initial praise of the excellence of the Dharma and the excellence of the Dharma-preacher. Within that section on resolving doubts, there are these four types of doubt; the first doubt concerns the granting of a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*). It asks: at what time was the preliminary method (*upāya*) first taught, and later was the reality (*tattva*) taught?
Since the second [person] harbored doubts regarding the prediction concerning rebirth in a higher realm and rose from his seat and departed out of overweening pride (*adhimāna*), how is this known?

If one follows the first interpretation, the third [person] harbored doubts regarding the prediction concerning the cause; for the Buddha’s mind was originally fixed on speaking for two types of persons and not for those who are deluded regarding the Dharma, and thus he gave rise to this doubt: "How can he possibly speak [of this]?"

If one follows the latter interpretation, it would also imply that the prediction concerns rebirth in the higher realms; yet, since the fourth doubt concerns rebirth in all higher realms, how could the initial statement and the subsequent statement not contradict each other? How, then, would this not constitute false speech?
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from “At that time, the World-Honored One went to the female lay devotee (upāsikā) who lacked faith,” the commentary states:

Among the one hundred and twenty-one verses that follow, the final three verses constitute the fourth section of this chapter. They encourage the arousal of a joyful mind so that she may know she shall become a Buddha. Thus, the first one hundred and eighteen verses comment upon the preceding prose, specifically the third part, which reveals this true reality (dharmatā) and opens the gate of provisional means (upāya). This section is divided into two parts:
The first one hundred and fifteen verses comment upon the two preceding predictions, while the final three verses comment upon the refutation of the four doubts.
Within the former section, there are again two parts:

the first four verses comment upon the departure from the assembly of evil persons during the taking of the prediction, and the subsequent one hundred and eleven verses comment upon the bestowing of the prediction.

Of the four [sections], the first verse praises those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*); the subsequent three verses praise those whose roots of transgression are deep and heavy. These four verses correspond respectively to pride, violation, concealment, and obstruction; this [first] verse concerns pride.

For those who have left the household life, the realization of the Path is paramount; yet they may consider a little attainment to be much, or give rise to overweening pride (*adhimāna*) upon attaining much.
Laymen, for the most part, are deeply attached to a self and harbor haughty hearts, thus giving rise to the conceit of "I am" (*asmimāna*).

Laywomen, for the most part, give rise to the pride of inferiority (*ūnamāna*), lacking confidence in the superior Path; they are slightly attached to a self, and even as they follow the company of their husbands, they harbor a lack of faith.
Regarding the sūtra passage, “In this way, the fourfold assembly and others have deficiencies and leaks in their precepts,” the commentary states:
The following three verses describe the profound and heavy roots of transgression, as they distinguish between the violation of precepts, the concealment of offenses, and the obstacles to the Dharma.

This constitutes a transgression of the precepts. A minor transgression is termed a "deficiency" (*chidra*), while a major transgression is termed a "leakage" (*asrava*), because both are subject to censure and reproach.

Violating the precepts is called a deficiency; violating the view is called a leakage. Alternatively, when the outflow of afflictions arises yet one fails to perceive it, maintaining a conceited mind and claiming to have attained saintly status—since the precepts state that such overweening pride (*adhimāna*) must be eliminated—one then commits a grave offense. Therefore, this is particularly egregious; it is not merely a case of the *śīla* (ethical discipline) being impure, for it falls under the category of the non-manifestation of *samādhi*.
Now, when it is said that they have violated the precepts, this is stated in general terms, and one does not know the specific characteristics of the violations.
As the Sūtra says: "They guarded and cherished their flaws until [the demons] departed because of the Buddha's majestic power."
The commentary states:
This refers to concealing one's offenses.
When there is internal disease within jade, it is called a flaw (*xiá*); when there is external blemish on jade, it is called a scar (*cǐ*). It is the same with the violation of precepts.
Worldly censure is like a flaw on the surface; internal arising of transgressions is like a blemish within; transgressions of body and speech are like *bi* (cracks), which are precisely "defects";
and transgressions of the inner mind are like *xia* (pores), which are precisely the aforementioned "leakages."

The transgression of a *prakṛti-sāvadya* (inherent offense) is termed a "flaw" (*kha*), while the transgression of a *pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya* (prohibited offense) is termed a "blemish" (*ci*). The term for external defects in jade should indeed be "blemish" (*ci*).

That it is currently written as "defect" (*cha*) is because those within the Dharma have the disease of afflictions; just as jade has flaws, this is a metaphorical teaching that aligns the phenomenon with the principle.
Because a flaw is a sickness, one guards it with care and does not expose it, concealing one's own failings.
Dregs of wine are called *zao* (dregs), because they are extremely heavy and turbid.
Rice husks are called *kang* (chaff), because they are light and useless.

Not only do those of inferior wisdom turn their backs on the Dharma and act according to their own whims, but the Buddha’s majestic power sweeps them away to compel them to depart. Fearing that if they were to hear the sublime Dharma, they would slander it and increase their transgressions—which would be of no benefit to them—he thus uses his majestic power to coerce them into rising and leaving.
Regarding the sūtra passage, “This person has meager merit... down to ‘there are only [those who possess] true reality,” the commentary states:
This refers to the obstruction of the Dharma (*dharmāvaraṇa*).

"In past lives, they created the karma of withholding the Dharma; with such Dharma-obstructions present in their bodies, they are incapable of hearing the Dharma, and thus [those who do hear it] are few.
Both "xiǎn" (rare) and "xiǎn" (few) are acceptable.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "Śāriputra, listen well" up to "and preach it for the sake of sentient beings," the commentary states:
The following second section, consisting of one hundred and eleven verses, praises [the Buddha] and bestows predictions of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
The prose version consists of six sections; here, too, it is divided into six:

first, six verses comment on the "Exposition"; next, seven and a half verses comment on "Causing to Abide"; next, one and a half verses comment on "Preventing"; next, eighteen and a half verses comment on "Based on What Meaning"; next, seventy and a half verses comment on "Based on the Dharma"; and finally, seven verses comment on "Causing to Hear What Was Not Heard."
Regarding the differences among the six [types of monks], there is a distinction between those who precede and those who follow;

thus the verse says: "Six are said to dwell for seven and a half [years]; Next, one verse and a half provides the prohibition; What are the eighteen and a half? Seventy and a half, and seven and two."
The first six verses are divided into two parts:

the first four and a half verses explain the text from "Why is this so? onwards, while the latter one and a half verses explain the preceding heading: "The underlying intention of what has been taught according to suitability is difficult to understand."
The beginning and middle [of this section] further consist of three parts:

the first verse praises "innumerable skillful means," while the second verse praises "various causes, conditions, parables, and expressions"—that is to say, parables, causes and conditions, contemplation, and skillful means.
The first and a half verses concern "the exposition of all dharmas.
This is the initial [section].

In the preceding prose, it was indicated as "that which the Buddhas have spoken according to what is appropriate," and in the commentary, it was stated as "I, by means of countless skillful means. Now, this verse explains it as "the dharma attained by the Buddhas through the power of immeasurable skillful means. Thus, the earlier and later parts illuminate one another, and the perspectives of others and oneself mutually clarify each other; they are not contradictory.
Regarding the passage from the Sūtra, “The thoughts of sentient beings... until causing all to rejoice,” the commentary says:
This praises the various causes and conditions, among which there are two parts.

The first verse knows the capacity [of the disciples], while the subsequent verses provide the causes, conditions, and analogies for the mental reflections, the practice of the path, and the universal application of conduct.
"Various desires" refers to the diverse inclinations.
"Various natures" refers to the diverse realms (*dhātu*).
"Virtuous and non-virtuous karma from previous lives" refers to the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna*) as well as one's own karma.

It speaks of the Buddha’s five powers of knowledge (*jñānabala*) and his various modes of mindfulness and contemplation; because he can know these five aspects regarding sentient beings, he teaches the Dharma through causes, conditions, parables, and skillful means (*upāya*), causing all to rejoice, thereby explaining the origin of the various expressions mentioned previously.
The Sūtra states: "From the *sūtra* up to the *upadeśa*.
The commentary says:
One verse or one and a half verses expound upon all phenomena (*dharmas*).
Based on the sequence of the twelve divisions of the scriptures as taught in various sources: first, the *sūtra*, which the scripture calls *sūtra*;
second, the *geya*, which the scripture calls *geya*;
third, the *vyākaraṇa*, which is not present here;
Fourth is *geya* (recitation), which the sutra calls *gāthā*;
fifth is *udāna* (spontaneous utterance), which is not present here;

sixth is *nidāna* (circumstantial origin), which the sutra calls *hetu-pratyaya*; seventh is *avadāna* (parable); eighth is *itivṛttaka* (past events); and ninth is *jātaka* (birth stories)—the names for these three are the same as those used here.
The "Extensive Teachings of the Ten Directions" (Daśadigvaipulya) are not included herein;
the "Eleven Rare Phenomena" (Ekādaśādbhutadharma) are what the Sūtra calls the "Unprecedented" (Adbhuta);
and the "Twelve Discourses on Discussion" (Upadeśa) are what the Sūtra calls the "Upadeśa-sūtras."
Regarding this meaning, it is analyzed through three gates:
first, the definition of its characteristics; second, the explanation of its name; and third, its classifications.
As for the definition of its characteristics, the sūtra has two characteristics:
There are two types: general and specific.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

"From 'Thus have I heard' up to 'rejoicing and practicing accordingly,' all such [texts] are called sūtras. This encompasses all twelve divisions of the teachings; this is termed their general characteristic, because the teaching penetrates both principle and the guidance of sentient beings.
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states:
"That which strings together prose to provide a concise exposition of the meanings that ought to be explained is called a *sūtra*; this refers exclusively to prose as its distinct characteristic.
Verses, however, do not [constitute the sūtra itself], as they are subsumed under a separate category of *sūtra*."
Geyas have two characteristics:
first, to benefit those who come later; second, to clarify meanings that were previously not fully understood.

The *Abhidharma* and other treatises state: "In various sūtras, when the meaning of the preceding prose is restated in verse, either in the middle or at the end, it is called 'benefiting those who come later.'"

It is further stated: "Sūtras of incomplete meaning (neyārtha) should be further explained through verse; although they are taught in prose, their meaning is not yet fully clarified, and thus they are called 'those that manifest previously unclarified meaning.'"
The *Nirvāṇa* [Sūtra] speaks only of the first of these meanings.
There are three types of prophetic declarations (*vyākaraṇa*):

first, the prediction of the causes and effects regarding the death and rebirth of disciples; second, the clear and explicit prediction of profound and secret meanings; and third, the prediction of the matter of bodhisattvas attaining Buddhahood.

The *Abhidharma* and other texts state: "In this regard, when noble disciples have passed away into the past, their virtues, faults, and the distinctions of their places of rebirth are prophesied. This refers to the prophecy of the causes and effects regarding the death and rebirth of disciples.

Furthermore, it says: "Moreover, the definitive sūtras are called vyākaraṇa (explanations), because they reveal and elucidate the profound and secret meaning. This refers to the second [type], which records the profound and secret meaning.
Therefore, this treatise states:
"There are four kinds of prophecy:
namely, the prophecy of a resolute mind, of causes, of grasping, and of bestowing."
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The Tathāgata bestows a prediction upon the great beings, saying: 'O Ajita!

In the future there shall be a king named Śaṅkha; in that world he shall attain Buddhahood and be named Maitreya. This is a sūtra of prediction," which constitutes the third prediction of his attainment of Buddhahood.

Regarding the characteristics of *geya* (versified exposition), the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* and other texts state: "It refers to those passages within the various sūtras that are not spoken in prose form, but are instead composed in verse, consisting of one line, or two, three, four, five, or six lines, all of which constitute *geya*."

Regarding the characteristics of the *svayambhāṣita* (self-spoken), the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other texts state: "That which is spoken without a formal request—being for the sake of causing the True Dharma to abide long and the True Teaching to abide long—is called *svayambhāṣita*."
There are three characteristics of the *nidāna* (causal origin):
first, teaching at the request of others; second, establishing precepts due to an offense; and third, teaching the Dharma in connection with specific events.
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states:

"Regarding 'causal conditions' (nidāna): it refers to teaching at the request [of others], as well as the establishment of training rules (śikṣāpada) due to specific causes and conditions. Thus, these first two meanings are termed "origination" (nidāna).
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"It is like the fundamental basis for the verses in various sūtras.

For instance, in the city of Śrāvastī, there was a man who caught birds with a net and then released them again. The World-Honored One, knowing the origins and conditions of this matter from beginning to end, spoke these verses:"
"Do not disregard a minor offense, thinking that it will bring no calamity; though a drop of water is minute, it gradually fills a large vessel.
This is called dependent origination (nidāna).
This is the third cause for teaching the Dharma.
Regarding the characteristics of parables (*dṛṣṭānta*), the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"It refers to the various parables found within the Sūtras and Vinaya that are used to explain all phenomena."
Regarding the characteristics of *pūrvayoga* (past lives), the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"It refers to all matters concerning persons or phenomena in the past, excluding the Buddha’s own birth stories (*jātaka*)."

In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it is taught that there are only dharmas that have passed away. For example, the Dharma I have preached since appearing in the world is called the *Dhātu-sūtra*; under Krukin Buddha it was called the *Amṛta-druma*; under Kanakamuni Buddha it was called the *Dharma-ādarśa*; and during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha it was called the *Vibhaṅga-śūnyatā*.
This does not refer to ordinary people, but is based on the universal application of the principle.
Regarding the characteristics of *jātaka* (birth stories), the *Xianyang lun* states:
"That which proclaims how the World-Honored One, in various places in the past, underwent death and birth, practicing the bodhisattva path and performing difficult practices—this is called *jātaka*."
"When it is said that the Buddha, while he was a bodhisattva, [performed] either bodily acts or deeds, these are all *pūrvajanmas* (former births).

In the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, only the former bodies of the bodhisattva are mentioned, not his former deeds, such as his becoming a deer, a bear, a roe deer, or a rabbit, and so on, up to the detailed accounts of his becoming a garuḍa and other such beings.
Vaipulya has two characteristics:
first, it expounds the path of the bodhisattva; second, its dharma is vast and manifold because it is extremely sublime and lofty, and because its duration is long.
While this [category] also applies to the Śrāvakas, who likewise possess Vaipulya, here we take the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, which possesses both characteristics, as the definitive standard.

Regarding "marvelous phenomena" (*adbhutadharma*): this refers to the common and uncommon virtues of all Buddhas and the eightfold assembly of noble disciples as proclaimed within the various sūtras, as well as other most excellent, extraordinary, and astonishing teachings; these constitute marvelous phenomena.

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* speaks exclusively of the Buddha’s deeds, such as when the Buddha first took seven steps immediately after birth, emitting a great radiance that illuminated the ten directions; the monkey offering honey; the white dog listening to the Dharma; and Māra transforming into a blue ox walking among the clay bowls, causing them to touch one another without being damaged.
It speaks only of the rare and marvelous events concerning disciples and non-disciples; all such instances are termed "rare dharmas" (adbhuta-dharma).
There are two characteristics of these discourses:
first, those spoken by the Buddha himself; second, those spoken by his disciples.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:

"It refers to the systematic investigation and examination of various sūtras; all sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) are called *mātṛkā*, because in these instances the Blessed One himself extensively analyzes the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*)."

Furthermore, when a noble disciple has already seen the path of the truths and, relying on their own realization, correctly discerns the essential nature of all phenomena, this is also called *mātṛkā* and is also called *abhidharma*.
For now, this citation is sufficient to encompass the full meaning; as for the remaining specific teachings, I fear they would be too prolix to cite.

Regarding the explanation of the names: first, I shall explain the general name. Previous masters translated it as "the twelve divisions of the sūtras" (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*). The term "division" (*aṅga*) contains two meanings:
first, a single unit; second, a category or class.
These are the categories, as there are distinctions among the twelve types of meaning.

Ancient scholars raised doubts, saying that the twelve divisions of the *piṭaka* scriptures led Daoists to speak of thirty-six divisions, with the followers of Laozi and Zhuangzi each constituting one division.
Regarding the current term "twelvefold teaching" (*dvādaśāṅga-śāsana*): "fold" (*aṅga*) refers to divisions, as there are twelve distinct divisions of both text and meaning.

Furthermore, the term "sūtra" (*jing*) is often conflated with *sūtra* (discourse); here it is translated as "teaching" (*jiao*), which serves as a general designation for all twelve parts without such confusion. This is an analysis based on the inclusion of a numerical value.

To explain the specific names, there are three general categories. The six names—*geya* (verses), *geya* (chanting), *udāna* (inspired utterances), *nidāna* (causal origins), *adbhutadharma* (marvelous phenomena), and *vaipulya* (extensive teachings)—are all *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compounds, because they refer respectively to "verses that should be repeated," and so on, up to "the extensiveness of the principle of the vast."
The category of *upadeśa* (treatise/discourse) is explained solely by the *karmadhāraya* compound, because the essence of the treatise is itself the discourse.

Alternatively, *geya* (recitation/chanting) may also be explained by the *karmadhāraya*, as it is that which can be chanted and recited; this differs from *geya* [in the sense of] *gāthā* (verse), because the former is the teaching (*deśanā*) while the latter is the verbal expression (*vacana*).

The five categories—Sūtra (契經), Vyākaraṇa (記別), Avadāna (譬喻), Itivṛttaka (本事), and Jātaka (本生)—are explained through both the *karmadhāraya* (持業) and *tatpuruṣa* (依主) compounds. "Sūtra" means that which accords [with reality]; it is a sūtra that accords with principle, and so on, up to "Jātaka," which means birth itself, or birth in a former life.
Regarding the distinctions, there are two: first, the distinction of essence; second, the distinction of teaching.

As for the distinction of essence: within *geya* (verses in response) there is definitely no *udāna* (inspired utterances), and within *udāna* there is definitely no *geya*, because their beginnings and endings differ, and because they differ in being single or repeated.
Within the *Itivṛttaka* (Past Events) there are certainly no *Jātaka* (Birth Stories), and within the *Jātaka* there are certainly no *Itivṛttaka*, because teacher and disciple are distinct.

These four sections possess only eleven [divisions], whereas the remaining eight sections all possess twelve, as they each contain the aforementioned specific characteristics according to their respective requirements.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"From 'Thus have I heard' at the beginning to 'so should one practice' at the end, all are sūtras. Therefore, [the definition] applies universally to all twelve divisions of the teachings;

yet, if taken in its specific sense, it excludes those that lack these features, as it refers exclusively to long prose discourses (*vaipulya*) as *sūtras*, whereby the two verses [defining *sūtra*] would no longer apply.
The remaining seven teachings all possess the twelve [aspects]; this may be understood by analogy.

Regarding the fact that the *geya* (verses) contain eleven [aspects], the "Parable Chapter" states: "Śāriputra shall become a Buddha in a future age, with the title of Universal Wisdom, named Flower Light, and shall deliver immeasurable multitudes. This is precisely the *geya* that includes *vyākaraṇa* (prophecy).

Within the *geya* (verses corresponding to prose) there are also instances of *udāna* (spontaneous utterances). As stated in the "Expedient Means" chapter: "The Hero of the World is immeasurable; among all classes of beings, including devas and humans, none are able to know the Buddha. This is precisely an *udāna* within the *geya*.

Within the *geya* (verses) there are also *nidāna* (introductory narratives). The *Upāyakauśalya-parivarta* states: "Śāriputra, listen well: the Dharma attained by all Buddhas is taught to sentient beings through immeasurable powers of skillful means. This is a *geya* that serves as a *nidāna*, for it was spoken in response to the request of Śāriputra.

Within the *geya* (verses of response) there are also parables; for instance, "Suppose there were an elder who had a large house, and that house was long-standing and moreover dilapidated," and so forth—this is a parable within the *geya*.

Within the *geya* (verses) there are also *itivṛttaka* (past events). As stated in the "Introductory Chapter": "After that Buddha passed into parinirvāṇa, you were the indolent one; the Dharma Master Varaprabha was none other than my own self. This is precisely a *geya* that recounts a past event.

Within the *geya* (verses) there are also *jātaka* (birth stories); the "Chapter on Never-Disparaging" states, "At that time, Never-Disparaging was none other than myself," which is precisely a *jātaka* presented as a *geya*.

Within the *geya* (verses) there are also *vaipulya* (extensive teachings); as the "Expedient Means" chapter states: "In the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the Single Vehicle Dharma; there is neither a second nor a third, except for what is taught through the Buddha’s expedient means. This is precisely a *vaipulya* verse within the *geya*.

Within the *geya* (verses) there are also rare events (*adbhutadharma*). The "City of Transformation" chapter states: "The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū sat at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas; yet the Buddha-dharma did not manifest before him, and he did not attain the path of Buddhahood. This is an example of a rare event within the *geya*.

Within the *geya* (verses) there are also *upadeśa* (expository discourses). The "Chapter on the Lifespan" states: "When sentient beings have gained faith and submission, being upright and gentle of mind, desiring with a single heart to see the Buddha and not begrudging their own bodies or lives, then I and the assembly of monks shall together emerge from Vulture Peak. At that time I will say to the sentient beings: 'I am always here and do not perish; by the power of skillful means, I manifest both extinction and non-extinction. This is an expository discourse within the *geya*."
The remaining three teachings all possess eleven divisions; this should be understood by analogy. However, this sutra contains all twelve divisions:

the entire work constitutes the *sūtra* (契經) in its general character; wherever this meaning is reiterated, it is the *geya* (應頌); wherever there are predictions (*vyākaraṇa*) or the exposition of profound meanings, these are the *vyākaraṇa* (記別); and in the "Parable of the Phantom City" chapter, where the Brahmā of the East speaks in verse, saying, "The World-Honored One is most rare, difficult to encounter; endowed with immeasurable merit, he is able to rescue and protect all," and so forth, these are all *gāthā* (諷頌).

The beginning of the "Expedient Means" chapter is an *autpattika* (self-proclaimed) discourse; thus, the preceding verse states: "Without being asked, he spoke spontaneously, extolling the path he himself had traversed. The three requests of Śāriputra, the three requests of Maitreya, and all other instances where the provisional and the ultimate are taught are likewise *nidāna* (circumstantial origins).
The "Parable Chapter" (*Avadāna-parivarta*) and others are all parables (*avadāna*).
Passages that recount the past lives of the various disciples are all "Past Events" (*itivṛttaka*).
Passages that recount the Buddha’s own past lives are all "Birth Stories" (*jātaka*).
All passages that teach the One Vehicle (ekayāna) are Vaipulya;
all passages that describe the manifestation of supernatural powers (ṛddhi) are Adbhutadharma;
and the section on the "Life Span" (*Āyuṣpramāṇa-parivarta*), in which the Buddha himself engages in dialogue to explain the characteristics of the three bodies (*trikāya*), may be termed Upadeśa.
Regarding the distinction of the teachings: there is one great [division] and nine small ones, which refers to the text of this very sutra.

The Hīnayāna lacks only three types—prophecies (*vyākaraṇa*), self-expositions (*udāna*), and extensive teachings (*vaipulya*)—but it does not preclude the existence of the twelve divisions within the Mahāyāna.

Regarding "two small, one complete, and nine large," the third fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Those who protect the Mahāyāna receive and uphold the ninefold division. This excludes the *nidāna*, *avadāna*, and *upadeśa*, yet it does not preclude the existence of the twelvefold division within the Śrāvaka vehicle.

Regarding the three large and eleven small [sections], the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (38) states: "One portion of the Vaipulya belongs exclusively to the Bodhisattva-piṭaka; the remaining portions belong to the Śrāvaka-piṭaka."

Regarding the "four greats and one small" (the five aggregates) and the eleven [bases], the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (85) states: "With the exception of a portion of the Vaipulya, the remainder is called the Sūtras associated with the Śrāvaka-yāna."
Why is this entire passage [classified as] the "Minor Nine"?
It is called *vyākaraṇa* (prediction) because it bestows upon disciples the prediction that they shall attain Buddhahood.
It is said that there is no such thing for Śrāvakas because they have not previously sought Great Bodhi; it is like showing a jewel to a fool, whereupon the fool laughs.
The same applies to the Śrāvakas receiving predictions; therefore, it is said that there are none. This does not mean that there is no prediction concerning the passing away and rebirth of disciples.

Furthermore, those of the Śrāvaka vehicle have heard only shallow teachings; if one were to preach to them without being requested, arrogance would arise. Thus, although it is said that there is no preaching of one's own accord, in reality, such exists.

Furthermore, while Śrāvakas realize only minor fruits and do not attain perfect enlightenment, their principles are not ultimate and their practices are not comprehensive; thus, they do not speak of the Vaipulya (the Extensive). Yet, in reality, there is indeed within their True Dharma the Vaipulya that extensively sets forth the teachings.
Therefore, in this verse, it is said that for the sake of the śrāvakas there are only nine divisions of the teachings; however, in principle, these extend to twelve.

Regarding the "small" and "complete" versions of the nine divisions mentioned in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, they are designated as "causes and conditions" (nidāna) because the precepts were established due to transgressions. Since bodhisattvas do not commit such transgressions, these are omitted and described as "non-existent"; this does not mean they lack the *nidāna*—the originative narrative of teaching the Dharma in response to a request based on specific events.

Now, the use of analogies is intended to instruct those of middling and inferior faculties; even for one of sharp and superior faculties such as Śāriputra, there are still many instances where he does not require an analogy, let alone the majority of Bodhisattvas who do not require them at all. Thus, while it is said that [analogies] are "non-existent" for them, in principle they do indeed exist.

Furthermore, the nature of great bodhisattvas is such that their faculties are all sharp; they understand the entire tenet system at once without needing to rely on cross-examination before the mind of wisdom arises. Thus, while it is said there is no formal debate, in reality, reasoning is not absent.

Furthermore, those who protect the Dharma mostly recite the Sūtra Piṭaka; the Nidāna and Avadāna are mostly included in the Vinaya Piṭaka; and the Upadeśa is mostly subsumed within the Abhidharma Piṭaka. Therefore, it is said that there are "only nine" great [treatises], yet logically it is not that there are not twelve.

Regarding the thirty-eight [categories] of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the eleventh of the eleven minor sections, even in the Hīnayāna there are records of disciples passing away; furthermore, because the Buddha’s compassion is so profound that he does not wait for a request, it includes both prophetic declarations (*vyākaraṇa*) and spontaneous discourses (*udāna*), thus totaling eleven categories.

Regarding those who lack the Vaipulya [sūtras]: they do not seek perfect enlightenment and their explanations of principle are coarse and shallow; thus they are termed "lacking," yet in reality they possess them as well.
The text of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 85, does not differ from what precedes it.

However, while the eleven [categories] are taught as the Śrāvaka-piṭaka, the Vaipulya is taught in contrast to them as the Bodhisattva-piṭaka; it is not that the Bodhisattva-piṭaka lacks the other eleven. Rather, these differences in enumeration are all spoken according to specific individual meanings. In reality, both the Śrāvaka and Bodhisattva piṭakas fully possess all twelve categories.
Now, following what is required, I shall provide a brief analysis; the remaining detailed explanations should be understood according to the respective chapters.
As for the sūtra passage: "For those of dull faculties who delight in inferior teachings... [it] is for them that I preach nirvāṇa."
The commentary states:
This one and a half verses clarify the meaning of what was previously indicated—that the underlying intent (*abhiprāya*) of the teachings given according to circumstances is difficult to understand.

Briefly, this is due to five reasons: first, those of dull faculties find it difficult to awaken; second, they delight in the small and fear the great; third, they are addicted to birth and death and do not fear the supramundane; fourth, they fail to practice when encountering favorable conditions; and fifth, they are currently oppressed by manifold sufferings.

Based on these five meanings, Nirvāṇa is taught for their sake; because they possess dull faculties, they are attached to saṃsāra. Although they encountered various Buddhas who had already transformed them in the past, they did not practice the profound and subtle path of the Mahāyāna. Due to their practice of evil, they fell back and suffered. Because [the Buddha] exhorted them to leave suffering behind, he initially taught them the Nirvāṇa of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha). Thus, the account at the beginning of the "Chapter on Faith and Understanding" (*Śraddhāparivarta*), where [the sons] encounter the Buddha and subsequently fall back into the flow of saṃsāra before being later transformed by the two vehicles, is precisely the same as this.
Regarding the passage from the Sūtra, “I shall employ this skillful means... until I attain the Buddha-way,” the commentary states:
The second section below consists of seven and a half verses; within the fourth [section], which causes [beings] to abide, there are four parts.
One verse provides the heading, one verse provides the explanation, half a verse constitutes the assembly, and one verse exhorts them to abide.
This is the first [section]. Initially, two provisional means are established in order to cause them to ultimately enter the Buddha-wisdom and abide in the One Vehicle.
Regarding the passage from the Sūtra, "The reason why [I] have never before spoken... up to 'definitively teaching the Mahāyāna,'" the commentary states:

This explains the preceding heading. It brings together what was said previously: "Your faculties were not yet mature and you had not awakened to the Mahāyāna; you were not fit to be taught. Now, your faculties are mature, and this is precisely the right time; therefore, it is being taught.
The same *Pariṇāmika-parivarta* states: "O bhikṣus!

When the Tathāgata knows for himself that the time for his parinirvāṇa has arrived, and when the assembly is pure, their faith and understanding firm, they have thoroughly realized the dharma of emptiness, and have entered deeply into meditative concentration—he then gathers the assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas and preaches this sūtra for them. In the world, there are no two vehicles by which one attains extinction; it is only through the single Buddha-vehicle that one attains extinction."
Regarding the passage from the Sūtra, “These ninefold teachings of mine... therefore I preach this sūtra,” the commentary states:
The following four and a half verses are divided into three sections.

One verse clarifies that the Lesser Dharma is not the true teaching and is designated as the "Root Text"; one and a half verses clarify that the Great Dharma is supreme and wondrous and is taught for superior persons; and two verses conclude by establishing the superiority of the person and the Dharma, exhorting the abandonment of the non-sublime person and Dharma.
This is the first [section].

These nine divisions were taught in accordance with the capacities of beginners; they serve as an entry point into the Great Text, yet are not the ultimate. Therefore, one should abide in the Great [Vehicle]. The Sūtra says:
"There are sons of the Buddha whose minds are pure... [down to] ...he preaches this Mahāyāna sūtra."
The commentary states:

The supreme and wondrous Great Dharma is proclaimed for the sake of superior persons; they are exhorted to abandon inferior teachings so as not to become evil persons. Whether through sudden or gradual enlightenment, all bodhisattvas are called children of the Buddha.
This possesses five virtues:
first, purity of mind, which consists in seeking exclusively the Mahāyāna wisdom of the Buddha rather than delighting in inferior paths, because it eliminates the two obstacles.
Second, a supple and humble mind that endures toil and fatigue, being capable of accomplishing great deeds through unremitting diligence.
Third, those of sharp faculties, whose nature is largely to uproot suffering and bestow happiness upon others, who are entirely impartial, and who swiftly enter the Dharma upon hearing it.
Fourth, those with the four immeasurables, who have long encountered favorable conditions under the Buddhas and constantly polish themselves.
Practicing the profound and wondrous path, they cultivate both merit and wisdom together, following the precious rules for attaining true awakening.
The *Bodhicittotpāda-sūtra* states that one who possesses ten qualities is capable of generating the bodhicitta:

first, associating with virtuous friends; second, making offerings to all Buddhas; third, cultivating roots of goodness; fourth, aspiring to seek the supreme Dharma; fifth, maintaining a mind that is always gentle and flexible; sixth, being able to endure suffering when encountered; seventh, possessing pure and profound compassion; eighth, having a deep mind of equanimity; ninth, loving and delighting in the Mahāyāna; and tenth, seeking the wisdom of the Buddha.
All are subsumed within these five: "purity of mind" subsumes two phrases—delighting in the Mahāyāna and seeking the Buddha’s wisdom;
"gentleness" subsumes two phrases:
The mind is always gentle and supple, capable of enduring suffering;
with sharp faculties, one embraces the two phrases:
compassion is profound and sincere, and the deep mind is impartial.
The two phrases subsumed by "immeasurable Buddhas" are:
drawing near to virtuous friends and making offerings to all Buddhas;
the two phrases subsumed by "practicing profound and wondrous supernormal powers" are:
They cultivate roots of goodness and aspire to seek the supreme Dharma.
One who possesses these five virtues becomes a son of the ten dharmas; only then should one preach the Mahāyāna to them, causing them to set out upon it.
The Sūtra states: "I grant this prediction that such a person shall attain [enlightenment]; therefore, I preach the Mahāyāna for them.
The commentary says:

This concludes the two exhortations to abandon what is not sublime and to embrace what is sublime; it records that a person endowed with the five virtues will become a Buddha in a future life, because they practice mindfulness of the Buddha with a profound mind and maintain pure precepts.
There are two ways of recollecting the Buddha:
first, verbal recollection; second, mental recollection.

In the former, one directs the mind toward the Buddha as a person, aspiring for his rescue and seeking his accomplishment; in the latter, through wisdom, one recollects the Buddha as the principle-body, seeking to realize it and eliminate obstacles.
Since their concentration and wisdom are thus, and they further maintain the pure precepts, the three trainings are perfected; therefore, he bestows upon them the prediction [of enlightenment].

These individuals, having heard that they shall attain Buddhahood, rejoice because it accords with their own minds. Since the Buddha already knows their minds, he speaks of the Great [Vehicle] for them.
The Sūtra says: "Whether śrāvakas or bodhisattvas, they will all undoubtedly attain Buddhahood.
The commentary states:
This is an exhortation to abide [in the path].
Praising the Dharma, explaining its benefits upon hearing it, and exhorting others to abide in the Mahāyāna.
From the Sūtra: “Within the Buddha-lands of the ten directions... leading sentient beings [to liberation].
The commentary says:
This third section, consisting of one and a half verses, refutes the sixth [position].
"Without two" means there is no second vehicle, the Pratyekabuddhayāna.
"Without three" means there is no third vehicle, the Śrāvakayāna.

From the superior toward the inferior, the Buddha Vehicle is primary; this is based on the truth that there is no duality of ultimate vehicles. This excludes provisional teachings, for within provisional teachings there may be three, as they employ three nominal designations to guide sentient beings.
The names "sheep" and "deer" are employed as provisional designations to lead [beings] out from the burning house; there are no two actual entities used to deliver sentient beings.

This teaching holds that both the *nirvāṇa* and *bodhi* of the Two Vehicles lack substantial reality and are both termed merely by provisional names. Nevertheless, while *nirvāṇa* can be realized through the removal of fetters, the Knowledge of All Modes (*sarvajñatā*) is not accomplished because of a lack of awakening. Therefore, they enter the "transformed city" to rest from suffering; though the sheep and deer have names, they do not actually ascend [to the ultimate goal].
Question:

Regarding the three matters termed "Great Parinirvāṇa," one who has merely attained liberation is said to have "entered the city"; one whose wisdom of the two emptinesses is called a "bull" has merely attained the superior "sheep or deer" of birth-wisdom.

Answer: Liberation from all suffering and its cessation is what is called entering the "Transformation City" (*nirmita-nagara*). This [wisdom] is absent in the Two Vehicles; therefore, they do not ascend the sheep or deer carts.

Furthermore, while liberation is shared with the Two Vehicles in its cessation of suffering, they also partially attain what is termed "entry. However, the category of True Wisdom (*tattvajñāna*) is uniquely perfected only by the Buddha; although they also partially attain it, it is not called "ascending. In principle, there is actually no distinction.

Furthermore, the afflictive obscurations and their causes and effects are all eliminated; liberation is called the "temporary entry" into the illusory city. The cognitive obscurations and their causes and effects are not extinguished; thus, regarding the two vehicles, it is not said that they have ascended to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from “Because of explaining the Buddha’s wisdom” to “thereby delivering sentient beings,” the commentary states:
The fourth section below consists of eighteen and a half verses, which comment upon the third [section], “Based on what meaning. This contains two parts:
One and a half verses mark the Great Matter; seventeen verses explain the opening, showing, awakening, and entering.
This is the first [section].

As previously stated, the Buddha’s wisdom comprises five types in total; here, however, it primarily discusses two dharmas of the Buddha-fruit—bodhi and nirvāṇa—which, as the nature of wisdom and the function of insight, together constitute "much wisdom. Alternatively, it may refer solely to true wisdom (*jñāna*) and not include suchness (*tathatā*).

The appearance of a Buddha in the world is for the purpose of manifesting this one [vehicle] so that beings may develop a joyful inclination toward it; this alone is the single reality, the ultimate, supreme, and unsurpassed fruit. The other two vehicles are not, in their essence, truly ultimate, supreme, or sublime. Therefore, in the subsequent sections of the sutra, when the first five perfections are compared with this sutra, the Prajñāpāramitā is not mentioned; thus, one never uses the Small Vehicle to save sentient beings.

Alternatively, this single entity is frequently described as having the nature of wisdom; as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* by Siṃhanāda: "Buddha-nature is emptiness, and emptiness is wisdom. Because of this, the nature of wisdom is also called wisdom itself.
Now, this text primarily adopts the first interpretation as correct, because the two vehicles do not exist [in that ultimate sense].
Since it states that the other two are not the truth, we know that this is not a case of negating the three to harmonize them into one in order to return to the One Vehicle.
Regarding the passage from the Sūtra, “The Buddha himself abides in the Great Vehicle... [and] by this he delivers sentient beings,” the commentary states:
The following seventeen verses explain the stages of opening, showing, awakening, and entering; these are divided into four parts.
One verse opens [the topic], five verses awaken [to it], one verse enters [it], and ten verses demonstrate [it].
This is the first [section].

In the Mahāyāna, the true principle (*tattva*) and correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna*) are taken together; the provisional designation "Buddha-body" eternally abides in this *nirvāṇa-bodhi*, which is termed "abiding. "Abiding" carries the meaning of relying upon and dwelling securely. What is attained is exclusively the true principle of the *dharmakāya*.

Alternatively, those of the Mahāyāna take only the ultimate truth; the realization and verification of this through correct wisdom is termed "abiding. Because this Dharma-body is fully endowed with all virtues and is the true nature of reality, the Buddha’s Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya)—just like the ultimate truth of the Dharma-body as it was realized—is further adorned with immeasurable concentration and wisdom. Concentration is merit (*puṇya*), and wisdom is knowledge (*jñāna*); together they encompass and sustain all conditioned virtues without exception.
Internally, one realizes the profound truth and fulfills *nirvāṇa*; consequently, true wisdom arises, and one becomes adorned with both merit and insight, thereby fulfilling *bodhi*.

Since one’s own virtues are thus perfected, one employs the two dharmas to open the way for sentient beings—this is called "deliverance"—and manifests that the nature of these two bodies is unsurpassed, so as to inspire joy in them.
Regarding the passage from "Having personally realized the unsurpassed path" to "this matter is impossible," the commentary states:
Below there are five verses; within these, three concern realization.
One and a half verses reveal equality; two and a half verses reveal supreme qualities; one verse brings about realization.
This is the first [section].
"Unsurpassed Way" refers to the excellence of correct wisdom; "unsurpassed Mahāyāna" refers to the excellence of ultimate truth.
First, the term "unsurpassed" (anuttara) permeates both locations; both are equal, being devoid of subject and object, and lacking any distinction between self and other or thing and self.

Furthermore, "Mahāyāna" refers to the unsurpassed path; because its application is supreme, once the Buddha has realized this wisdom and principle of equality, how could there be any dual distinction between self and other, or between things and the self?

If internal wisdom is unequal and one takes up the Mahāyāna for oneself alone, while external wisdom is unequal and causes others to take up the Hīnayāna, then one falls into the stinginess of withholding the Dharma (*dharmamātsarya*). Since the delusions of craving for fame and profit have not yet been exhausted, how can this be called attaining the realization of the Mahāyāna that universally carries all?
This is untenable. The Sūtra states:
"If a person has faith and takes refuge in the Buddha, they shall alone be without fear.
The commentary says:
The final two and a half verses reveal his supreme qualities, which are twofold:

the first one and a half verses reveal the quality of internal freedom from defilement and fearlessness, while the latter verse reveals the quality of external adornment and the teaching of the true Dharma.
This is the first [point].
"If a person has faith in the Buddha" refers to the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*).

"Taking refuge in the Buddha" refers to the subsequent cultivation of correct practice. The Tathāgata does not deceive, oppress, or treat them with contempt, nor does he bestow a minor teaching instead of a great one; he neither misleads nor deters them, nor does he promise a great teaching at the outset and fail to grant it later.

Why is this so? Because the Buddha neither covets nor begrudges the Mahāyāna such that he would deceive others by withholding it, nor does he harbor jealousy or fear that others might realize the Great Vehicle such that he would deceive or ensnare them; this is because he has severed all forms of evil within all phenomena.

Because the evil factors of afflictions, karma, and suffering—the unwholesome dharmas of birth and death—have been forever severed, and because he is devoid of all such matters as described above and possesses the perfection of right knowledge, he has no fear whatsoever throughout the ten directions; he utters the lion’s roar, declaring: "I am the All-Knowing One, the All-Seeing One, the Equal Transformer."
If there were superior matters remaining—such that evil was not yet exhausted and the fruit of wisdom was not yet perfected—how could one issue the roar of fearlessness throughout the ten directions?
Therefore, as it is said in the world: "When a father hears his son is hale and strong, he regrets not having killed himself; how could he begrudge anything else? Thus, there is no greed or envy.
The Sūtra states: "By means of my body adorned with the marks... up to... I shall preach for them the Seal of the True Nature.
The Commentary says:

This reveals the excellence of the true Dharma through external adornment; his physical frame is made majestic by the primary and secondary marks, and the radiance of his body and the radiance of his wisdom further illuminate both types of worlds—the vessel-world and the sentient-being-world. Because of this, all people revere him, and he is named the Knower of the World (*lokavid*).

If there is defilement within, there is no such sign externally; if such a sign appears externally, it clarifies that there is no defilement within. Therefore, I now speak of the Seal of the True Nature (*tathatā-mudrā*).
The Seal of the True Nature refers to the principle of the Mahāyāna of the two kinds of emptiness, for this principle serves as the seal that stamps the Great Teaching.
The Great Teaching is definitively supreme and real, not provisional; it is like the teaching in the Hīnayāna where the three seals of the Dharma are used to seal and determine the doctrine.
As the Sūtra says: "Śāriputra, you should know... [up to] ...it is no different from us."
The commentary says:
This verse is intended to bring about realization, such that you should realize the true wisdom of the Mahāyāna that was previously unknown to you, just as I have realized it.
For I formerly made a vow, desiring that all sentient beings be no different from myself, and wishing to cause them to realize this.
May it have faith, aspiration, and resolute conviction as its nature.
Regarding the Sūtra passage, “As I have previously vowed... until leading all to enter the Buddha-way,” the commentary states:
This single verse causes [beings] to enter; now that the fruit is fulfilled and his former vow-mind realized, he transforms sentient beings so they may enter the Buddha-way.
"Way" (mārga) has the sense of a cause, for it causes them to enter the eighth stage or the non-retrogressive stages from the first bhūmi upward, as these are the causes of Buddhahood.
Regarding the sūtra passage: "If I encounter sentient beings... up to being deluded and refusing instruction," the commentary states:
Below are ten verses of exposition, which are divided into two parts.
The first eight verses demonstrate that the beginning is not the same, while the final two verses demonstrate that the end returns to being the same.
Within the first section, there are three parts:
one verse demonstrates the meaning of "not being the same," six verses demonstrate the characteristics of "not being the same," and one verse concludes the section on "not being the same."
This is the first point.
If one were to teach all sentient beings exclusively through the Mahāyāna, this would be appropriate for those with wisdom;

however, ignorant fools might study erroneously and act in confusion. Their minds being deluded, they lack faith, harboring doubts, slandering, and thereby instead increasing their evil. They are unable to receive [the teaching], just as pouring water onto an overturned vessel or a puddle causes the vessel to become clogged; because this results in increasing the faults of the ignorant, one does not purely teach and transform them using only the Mahāyāna.
The Sūtra states: “I know that these sentient beings, due to delusion and craving, give rise to affliction.
The commentary says:
The following six verses demonstrate the characteristics of their differences, which are divided into two parts.

The first verse indicates that they are not the same because there is evil but no goodness; the subsequent five verses explain that they are not the same because there is evil but no goodness. This is the first [verse].

"Never having cultivated the roots of goodness" refers to the mundane skillful roots (*kuśalamūla*) that serve as the expedient means for transcending the world. Although these have arisen frequently since beginningless time, they are for the most part obscure and inferior; there is only innate goodness (*upapattilābhika-kuśala*), and no cause for outflow-free goodness (*anāsrava*). Because one is attached to the five sensory objects and clings to them without relinquishing them, with this as a condition, delusion (*moha*) gives rise to karma, and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) moistens rebirth.

Therefore, all the branches of birth, aging, and death within the cycle of rebirth cause the tree of suffering to grow. This occurs because there is a lack of the roots of goodness that serve as worldly-transcending expedients; with ignorance (*moha*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) acting as its two causes, one clings to the objects of the five desires and refuses to relinquish them. The ignorance that initiates karma generally arises from delusion regarding the internal [self], while the craving that moistens rebirth mostly arises in dependence on the five desires. Now, based on the desire realm, it is said in general terms that ignorance initiates karma through "clinging to desire," as this refers to the most prominent aspect.
The Sūtra states: "By means of the causes and conditions of various desires, one constantly increases [them] from lifetime to lifetime.
The commentary says:
The following five verses explain that there is evil and no goodness, and thus they are not the same; within these, there are two parts.
The first four verses differ because they involve evil; the final verse differs because it lacks goodness.
Within the former group, there are two parts:

the first one and a half verses differ because they involve being submerged in the five desires of the secular world; the latter two and a half verses differ because they involve seeking a false liberation through erroneous practice and confused study.
This is the first point.

Due to various desires, one purely gives rise to unwholesome karma and falls into the evil realms; due to mixed karma, one transmigrates through the six destinies and undergoes all manner of suffering. Since there is karma for birth and growth throughout the four modes of birth, and because one is oppressed by the three sufferings, the eight sufferings, and the five sufferings, the text specifically points to the manifest suffering of a single lifetime to make its argument; thus it says: "The subtle form received at conception grows constantly from life to life."
"Subtle" (miao) means inferior (lie).
"Womb" (tai) refers to the fetal sac; it is so called because it is enveloped in impurity, is loathsome and detestable, and because that which is subtle and inferior is born therein.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that those who are first taking birth originally reside in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). The maximum duration of this intermediate state is seven days; even at its longest, it does not exceed forty-nine days. For those who have committed evil deeds, the intermediate state appears like the light of a black sheep or a dark, cloudy night; for those who have performed virtuous deeds, it is like the light of white garments or a clear, bright night. They dwell there without obstruction, perceiving their future kin and the place of their rebirth. Those who have committed evil deeds look down with impure eyes and move with their faces cast downward. Those bound for the heavenly realms move with their faces turned upward; those bound for the human realm move with their faces turned sideways. If one has committed unwholesome conduct and is to be born in hell, they see their former companions and, filled with joy, rush toward them, only to be obstructed. This is likewise true for those in the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*) and the animal realm (*tiryagyoni*), which are characterized by pure suffering.

If there are other miscellaneous karmas, according to whether those karmas are wholesome or unwholesome, one will be born in a corresponding place; there, one feels sorrow or joy toward the parents—depending on whether they are male or female—which moistens the state of being about to be born. Grasping at the physical remains of the parents, at the moment of deluded intoxication, one is then constrained by them.

Within the first seven days, it is called *kalala*, which is translated here as "impure mixture. It is termed "mixture" because it is a combination of the impurities of the father and mother; it is termed "loathsome" because it is utterly disgusting, being like a congealed arrowhead that is thin inside.

Within the second seven-day period, it is called *arbuda*, which is translated as "blister"; its shape is like a blister on a pea, for its inner and outer surfaces are like curd and have not yet developed flesh.

Within the first twenty-one days, it is called *piśācika*, which here means "coagulation," because it is like blood that has begun to coagulate; in the Western Regions, this term for coagulated blood is called *piśācika*. If it has already become flesh, it remains extremely soft and supple.

Within the fourth seven-day period, it is called *ghanam*, which here means "coagulated thickness"; because it gradually becomes coagulated and thick, if it has already become firm and dense, it can slightly withstand touch.

Within the fifth seven-day period, it is called *praśākhā*, which here means "the stage of form"; it is like a lump of clay with five parts connected as one body and four limbs. Because the internal winds strike outward to produce the distinct characteristics of the sense organs and forms, the previously existing mass of flesh increases and the features of the various limbs appear.
Within six or seven days, it is called the stage of hair, body hair, and nails, because hair and body hair begin to grow.
Within seven weeks, it is called the stage of possessing the sense organs, because the five faculties become fully developed, clear, and prominent.
From this point, for another three months, he undergoes various developments without increase or decrease.

Thus, having completed thirty-eight weeks in the womb, after four further days have passed, his head turns downward and his feet turn upward; the fetal membrane then ruptures, and he is driven toward the birth canal. At that time, amidst the intense pressure and various sufferings, it may be that due to the mother’s prior karma of consuming ash or salt, the child’s hair and body hair are sparse;
or due to the mother’s prior karma of consuming warm or hot food, the child is born with a dark complexion or a reddish hue.
Alternatively, due to past karma, if the mother eats cold food or stays near a cold chamber, the child will often be dull-witted and pale;
if the mother indulges in sexual desire, the child will often suffer from scabies, leprosy, ringworm, and other such ailments;
if the mother frequently leaps and bounds and lacks dignified decorum, the child’s limbs will be deficient, deformed, and unsteady.

The male resides on the right side, leaning against the abdomen and facing the spine; the female resides on the left side, leaning against the spine and facing the abdomen. Because they conceive an affectionate attachment toward their parents, they first take up the impurities of the parents to form a body, and subsequently use the mother's impurities as sustenance for growth. Since the present conditions are thus, and because their karma is unwholesome, they are produced by a hundred evils with a body consisting of thirty-six impure substances. Such an evil body is not to be cherished; its ceaseless wandering through births is called "growing from life to life."
Regarding the sūtra passage from "Those of meager virtue and little merit" to "deceitful and crooked in mind, lacking sincerity," the commentary states:
These two and a half verses differ [from the preceding] because they concern seeking a false deliverance through erroneous practice and confused study.

The first one and a half verses clarify how the arising of wrong views regarding the self results in the sixty-two views; the subsequent verse explains how, due to the arising of the grasping at views and precepts, the remaining afflictions are produced.
Alternatively, the first verse generally clarifies the arising of the five views, while the subsequent one and a half verses specifically clarify the arising of the five views.

Since beginningless time, those sentient beings—due to their meager virtue and scant merit—have been oppressed by suffering; though they pray for deliverance, they do not discern the heterodox from the orthodox. They mistakenly enter into the improper views of external paths, and their erroneous practice and study are termed "false view" (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
